text: The catalog, the value versions and the five operations stay with P3 rwb-case under the R-PREC default ruling; the library only reads them through the published contract and holds no copy.
why: Template and Rules section R3 puts parameters and reference data (E1-042, E1-043) with rwb-case and DP-06 names the rwb-case parameters contract as the dependency; no source gives the platform library a schema, a store or a REST base, so a library that held the catalog would invent a service identity for itself.

text: The client keeps the legacy behaviour: a typed read that answers the value with its version number and resolves the business date, the product group and the environment; a cache refreshed on the owner's approval event and otherwise by its time to live; and a start-up refusal when a required value has no value for the environment.
why: The legacy story fixes that behaviour in its flow and criteria and the realignment changes the storage, not the behaviour (U2); without this default the contract would have to invent a new semantics for a reader that 19 services already depend on.

text: The two build checks stay with the library and are applied by the service template: RwbMagicNumberCheck allows 0, 1, -1 and test code and names the catalog key whose default equals the literal, and CatalogCompletenessCheck compares the keys read with the catalog file and fails on a missing key, owner or default.
why: The legacy story describes both checks in prose and places them in the monolith's build tools; in the target a check that fails a service's build cannot be owned by the owner of the catalog, and nineteen copies of the rule would drift.

impact: Which builds fail and on what finding shape; no business rule changes

text: The approval event keeps the legacy name and travels as rwb.case.ParameterVersionApproved.v1 on the owner's topic rwb.case.events.v1 by section R4 naming.
why: Legacy section 12 calls the event ParameterVersionApproved and names no topic, while section R4 fixes rwb.<short>.<Event>.v1 on rwb.<short>.events.v1; the owner is rwb-case, so the name follows from the ruling and no source states it.

text: The contract is published as one versioned artefact at major version 1, carrying the interface, the four types, the generated key set, the catalog and value data contract with DF-REF-132 to DF-REF-158, the four consumed operations, the event, the cache and start-up rules and the two build-check contracts, and it is frozen when the consuming stories pass their drift tests.
why: No source defines a published contract artefact for the client or its compatibility rule, and nineteen services cannot build against prose; the platform pattern of DP-11 requires a published contract with a mock before code.

text: The environment name, the cache time to live and the catalog file are chart values and the time to live is itself a catalog entry: the chart holds RWB_ENV, RWB_PARAMETER_CATALOG and RWB_PARAMETER_TTL_KEY plus a bootstrap value that is compared with refdata.cache.ttl-seconds at deployment, and from the first catalog answer the catalog entry governs.
why: The legacy story requires a value change with no release and makes the cache time to live a catalog entry, while a cache cannot ask the catalog for its own time to live before it has read anything; the split between a bootstrap value and the governing entry is the only reading that satisfies both.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 3 (refdata.cache.ttl-seconds default 300, 30 in SIT), section 4 step 8 and section 13 (cache time to live as a catalog entry; config.cache.ttl-seconds = 60 assumed; DL11); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 38 (one Helm chart and the golden pipeline in wave 0)
confirm: Platform team and the DevOps team at the chart review
impact: The chart values and the cache lifetime per environment; no business value changes

text: The seed job runs before the pods, the readiness probe reads the same check as the start-up check, and the three alerts are raised from the library's own metrics: a missing required value pages, a cache older than its time to live warns, and a failed refresh warns with the breaker state.
why: No source states the seed order, the probe or the alert thresholds, and without one order a service can start before the values it requires exist and serve traffic with nothing; the legacy story requires the refusal but not the mechanism.
read: RWB-E1-042 section 4 step 4, section 5 X3 and section 13 (parameter seed migration, ParameterStartupCheck as a health indicator); Architecture v5 Text Extract v1 slide 20 (/health and /metrics for the platform, every service)
confirm: Platform team, the DevOps team and the observability baseline owner at the SIT rehearsal
impact: The order of a release, the probe behaviour and the alert routes; no business value changes
